lead: A periodic discrete-time sequence repeats every N samples. The discrete-time Fourier series writes it as a sum of exactly N complex exponentials. The coefficients X[k] tell how much of each discrete frequency is present. This matters because digital filters, OFDM radios, and spectrum displays process blocks of samples, and the transform must respect the fact that a sampled sinusoid has only N distinct frequencies. The next chapters turn this finite series into the discrete-time Fourier transform (DTFT) and the discrete Fourier transform (DFT).
prereq: You need periodic signals and even/odd symmetry from Unit 1, the continuous-time Fourier series idea from Unit 3, and discrete-time sequences from Unit 5; the aperiodic case is in chapter 6.2.

blocks.text: Take a sequence x[n] that repeats every N samples: x[n+N] = x[n]. N is the period in samples. The discrete-time Fourier series (DTFS) writes one period as a sum of N complex exponentials e<sup>j2πkn/N</sup>, k = 0, 1, …, N−1. The integer k is the harmonic index: k=1 makes one cycle across N samples, k=2 makes two cycles, and so on. X[k] is a complex coefficient. |X[k]| is its amplitude and ∠X[k] is its phase in radians. j is the imaginary unit, j² = −1. The symbol Σ means sum.

blocks.where: X[k] is the coefficient of harmonic k; x[n] is one period; N is the period in samples; n runs from 0 to N−1.
The 1/N factor is the convention used here; k runs over the N harmonics.

blocks.text: The analysis equation gives X[k] from one period. The synthesis equation returns x[n] from all N coefficients. They are a DTFS pair.

Only N distinct exponentials exist. Add N to k: e<sup>j2π(k+N)n/N</sup> = e<sup>j2πkn/N</sup> e<sup>j2πn</sup> = e<sup>j2πkn/N</sup>, because n is an integer. Therefore X[k+N] = X[k]. The coefficients repeat every N. A continuous-time Fourier series has infinitely many harmonics; a sampled periodic sequence has exactly N.

For real x[n], X[N−k] = X*[k]. The star means complex conjugate: negate the imaginary part. X*[k] = Σ x[n] e<sup>j2πkn/N</sup>; the exponent equals e<sup>−j2π(N−k)n/N</sup>, so the sum is X[N−k]. This halves the independent coefficients. X[0] is real; for even N, X[N/2] is also real.

blocks.where: Holds when x[n] is real; X*[k] is the complex conjugate of X[k].

blocks.text: Parseval's relation fixes average power: P<sub>avg</sub> = (1/N) Σ<sub>n=0</sub><sup>N−1</sup> |x[n]|² = (1/N²) Σ<sub>k=0</sub><sup>N−1</sup> |X[k]|². The first sum uses time samples; the second uses harmonics. The 1/N², not 1/N, follows from the 1/N in synthesis. One period's energy is N·P<sub>avg</sub>.

Pulse train: x[n]=1 for n=0,1,2 and 0 for n=3,…,7, repeated with N=8. Its average power is 3/8 = 0.375. The worked example computes its coefficients; the figure lists |X[k]| for k=0,…,7. The marked values at k=1 and k=7 are equal because X[7]=X*[1].

Only k=0,…,N−1 are new. The discrete frequency of harmonic k is Ω<sub>k</sub> = 2πk/N radians per sample. For even N, k=N/2 gives π radians per sample, the fastest change a sampled sequence can show. k>N/2 repeats negative frequencies: k=N−1 is −2π/N radians per sample.

Some syllabi call this the discrete Fourier series (DFS). Some put 1/N on the analysis equation. Both conventions give the same x[n]. State your convention first. Here 1/N is on synthesis, so X[0] is the sum of one period, not the average.

To compute by hand: write one period x[0] to x[N−1]; compute X[0] as the plain sum; compute X[k] for k=1,…,N−1; use X[N−k]=X*[k] for real signals; check synthesis. The next chapter 6.2 lets N go to infinity and replaces the finite sum with the DTFT. The DFT appears in 6.3.

figure.caption: The two marked magnitudes are equal: X[k] repeats every N, and X[N−k] is the conjugate of X[k].

examples.question: A real periodic sequence has period N = 8. One period is x[0]=x[1]=x[2]=1 and x[3]=…=x[7]=0. Compute X[0], X[1], X[2], X[3] using X[k]=Σ<sub>n=0</sub><sup>7</sup> x[n]e<sup>−j2πkn/8</sup>. Then verify X[7]=X*[1].
steps: Write the three nonzero terms: X[k] = 1 + e<sup>−jπk/4</sup> + e<sup>−jπk/2</sup>, because 2πkn/8 = πkn/4.
X[2] = 1 + e<sup>−jπ/2</sup> + e<sup>−jπ</sup> = 1 − j − 1 = −j. Real part 0, imaginary part −1.
examples.check:
import cmath
N = 8
x = [1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
def X(k):
    return sum(x[n] * cmath.exp(-2j * cmath.pi * k * n / N) for n in range(N))
def clean(v):
    v = round(v, 6)
    return 0.0 if v == 0 else v
X0 = X(0).real
X1 = X(1)
X2 = X(2)
X3 = X(3)
X7 = X(7)
print(round(X0, 6))
print(round(abs(X1), 6))
print(round(cmath.phase(X1), 6))
print(clean(X2.real))
print(clean(X2.imag))
print(clean(X3.real))
print(clean(X3.imag))
print(clean(X7.real))
print(clean(X7.imag))

traps: Reading k past N−1 and expecting zero: X[N]=X[0], X[N+1]=X[1], and so on. The coefficient sequence is periodic.
Putting the 1/N factor on the wrong equation. Some books put it on analysis, so X[0] becomes the average. State the convention before computing.
Forgetting that with 1/N on synthesis, X[0] is the sum of one period, not the average. For the pulse train X[0]=3, not 0.375.
Using continuous-time harmonic counting. A sampled period has only N distinct frequencies; k=N/2 is the highest for even N.
Applying X[N−k]=X*[k] to a complex-valued x[n]. The conjugate symmetry holds only for real sequences.

quiz.q: State the DTFS analysis and synthesis equations for period N. Define N and k.
quiz.a: Analysis: X[k] = Σ<sub>n=0</sub><sup>N−1</sup> x[n]e<sup>−j2πkn/N</sup>. Synthesis: x[n] = (1/N)Σ<sub>k=0</sub><sup>N−1</sup> X[k]e<sup>j2πkn/N</sup>. N is the period in samples; k is the harmonic index from 0 to N−1.

quiz.q: Why is X[k] periodic with period N?
quiz.a: Adding N to k changes the exponent by e<sup>j2πn</sup>, which equals 1 for integer n. So X[k+N]=X[k].

quiz.q: For N=4, x[0]=x[1]=1 and x[2]=x[3]=0. Find X[0], X[1], X[2], X[3] using the analysis equation.
A student says X[9] for N=8 must be zero because 9 is outside 0,…,7. Correct or not?
quiz.a: Not correct. X[9]=X[8+1]=X[1]. Coefficients repeat every N; they do not become zero outside one period.

quiz.q: Write Parseval's relation for the DTFS and explain the 1/N² factor.
quiz.a: P<sub>avg</sub> = (1/N)Σ|x[n]|² = (1/N²)Σ|X[k]|². The 1/N² comes from the 1/N in the synthesis equation, which is squared in power.

quiz.q: For a real sequence with N=8, X[2]=−j. Find X[6] without recomputing the sum.
quiz.a: Use X[N−k]=X*[k]. Here N−2=6, so X[6]=X*[2]=j.

beyond: Not for the exam. In OFDM, data symbols sit on N subcarriers and an inverse DFT makes the time samples; a cyclic prefix then absorbs multipath echoes. A spectrum display often plots |X[k]| from the same finite sum. Circular convolution, which follows from the DTFS, is the basis of fast filtering with the FFT. Search next for DTFS, OFDM subcarriers, and circular convolution.
